ety.text: From Middle English rippen, from earlier ryppen (“to pluck”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rupjaną, *ruppōną, intensive of *raupijaną, causative of Proto-Indo-European *roub- ~ *reub-, variant of *Hrewp- (“to break”). See also West Frisian rippe, ripje, roppe, ropje (“to rip”), Dutch dialectal rippen, Low German ruppen, German Low German röpen, German rupfen, also Old English rīpan, rīepan (“to plunder”), West Frisian rippe (“to rip, tear”), German raufen (“to rip”); also Albanian rrabe ‘maquis’, possibly Latin rubus (“bramble”). More at reave, rob.
Uncertain; perhaps a variant of rep (“reprobate”).

senses.d: To divide or separate the parts of (especially something flimsy, such as paper or fabric), by cutting or tearing; to tear off or out by violence.
ex: to rip a garment; to rip up a floor

senses.d: To tear apart; to rapidly become two parts.
ex: My shirt ripped when it was caught on a bramble.

senses.d: To remove violently or wrongly.
ex: A child untimely ripped from its parents' arms.

senses.d: To get by, or as if by, cutting or tearing.
ex: He'll rip the fatal secret from her heart.

senses.d: To move quickly and destructively.
ex: The tornado ripped through northern Nebraska.
“Wall,” said the landlord, fetching a long breath, “that’s a purty long sarmon for a chap that rips a little now and then. ..."

senses.d: To cut wood along (parallel to) the grain.
To copy data from a CD, DVD, Internet stream, etc., to a hard drive, portable device, etc.
To take a hit, dose or shot of a drug (such as marijuana) or alcohol.
ex: He spent the day ripping shots at the bar and ripping blunts at home.
"... ripping shots of Jack Daniel's and vomiting in the bathroom.”

senses.d: To fart audibly.

A tear (in paper, etc.).

A comical, embarrassing, or hypocritical event or action.
A hit (dose) of marijuana.
A black mark given for substandard schoolwork.
Something unfairly expensive, a rip-off.
Data or audio copied from a CD, DVD, Internet stream, etc. to a hard drive, portable device, etc.

senses.d: A fart.
Something ripped off or stolen; a work resulting from plagiarism.
A worthless horse; a nag.
An immoral man; a rake, a scoundrel.
ex: Miss Compton, in 'Other People's Worries,' asks rhetorically whether a young rip was not in the Blank divorce case.

ety.text: From Middle English ripe, rype, from Old English rīpe (“ripe, mature”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīpī, from Proto-Germanic *rīpijaz, *rīpiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reyb- (“to snatch”). Cognate with West Frisian ryp (“ripe”), Dutch rijp (“ripe”), German reif (“ripe”). Related to reap.
From Middle English ripe, from Latin ripa.
An alteration of rife.

senses.d: Of a fruit, vegetable, seed, etc., ready for reaping or gathering; having attained perfection; mature.
ex: ripe grain
ripe apples

senses.d: Of a food, advanced to the state of fitness for use; mellow.
ex: ripe cheese

senses.d: Having attained its full development; mature; perfected.
ex: He was a scholar, and a ripe and good one.

senses.d: Of a person, ready, willing, eager.
ex: I'm starting somethin' myself. I'm ripe to fight. It's this country air!
